title: Europe's EV Market Sets a September Record as Global Sales Slip
dek: Nearly 600,000 EVs sold across Europe in September, while global demand fell 2% year over year. The divergent regions make it risky to tell a single growth story about automakers.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: Electric cars plugged into public charging points

keyPoints: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence counted 2.15 million global EV sales in September, down 2% year over year.
Europe sold almost 600,000 EVs, a record, with sales up 39% year over year and battery-electric volume up 50%.
North American EV sales fell 44% year over year as last September's U.S. federal tax-credit deadline created an unusually strong comparison.
body:
The global electric-vehicle market delivered a split-screen signal in September: European demand surged to a record, while sales worldwide declined from a year earlier. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence counted 2.15 million EVs sold globally, up 17% from August but down 2% year over year. Year-to-date global sales reached 15.5 million, 3% above the same nine-month period in 2025.

## Europe leads, but the comparison is not universal

Europe sold almost 600,000 EVs in September, 39% more than a year earlier, Benchmark said. Battery-electric vehicles rose 50%, while plug-in hybrids gained 16%. The International Council on Clean Transportation's September market monitor independently estimated that battery-electric vehicles made up 31% of new European registrations that month, with an average 24% share through January to September. Those measures differ in geographic coverage and methodology, so they should not be blended into one exact total; they point in the same direction: electrified cars took a larger portion of Europe's market.

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association reported that battery-electric cars accounted for 22.7% of EU registrations year to date through September, compared with 16.1% a year earlier. Its EU scope is narrower than the ICCT monitor's Europe-wide coverage. The association also found growth in France and Germany, where registrations of battery-electric cars were up 79.1% and 58.1% respectively over the first nine months. More model availability, national incentives and changes in fuel and energy costs all affect purchase decisions; no single factor explains the jump.

## North America and China pull the world total down

Benchmark attributed the worldwide year-over-year drop mainly to North America and China. North American sales fell 44%, the steepest regional decline of the year, after a rush of U.S. purchases in September 2025 ahead of the federal EV tax credit's expiration. That makes the current comparison unusually difficult and may improve mechanically in the fourth quarter as the baseline shifts to the post-credit slump. A better comparison would not necessarily mean renewed underlying growth.

China's domestic market was down 18% year over year in September, even as its passenger-car new-energy-vehicle exports reached a monthly record 558,000. Chinese manufacturers maintaining production while domestic demand weakened have sent more vehicles overseas, increasing competitive pressure on other markets. The distinction between local purchases and exports is crucial: a weak home market can coexist with rising export volumes.

## What automakers should take from it

The data do not support a single global verdict that EV adoption is either accelerating everywhere or stalling everywhere. They show regional differences in policy support, timing, affordability, supply, and the prior year's comparison. For automakers, Europe looks like a market where a broader electric lineup can capture expanding demand, while the North American decline warns that tax incentives and timing can shift deliveries across quarters. China's export growth adds competition on price and model range.

For investors, the next useful evidence is company-level deliveries, pricing and margins in each region. Aggregate sales growth is not enough to identify which manufacturer is gaining share or whether a higher EV mix is profitable. Benchmark's global headline is a reminder to watch geography carefully: a record in one region can be more than offset by a pullback elsewhere. Sources: [Benchmark Mineral Intelligence's September EV sales report](https://source.benchmarkminerals.com/article/global-ev-sales-reach-2-15-million-units-in-september-2026), [ACEA's September registration release](https://www.acea.auto/pc-registrations/new-car-registrations-5-7-in-september-2026-year-to-date-battery-electric-22-7-market-share/), [ICCT's September European market monitor](https://theicct.org/publication/european-car-market-monitor-september-2026/), and [Reuters' European sales coverage](https://www.reuters.com/business/europe-ev-sales-rose-70-september-almost-30-market-share-2026-10-19/).

marketImpact.summary: Europe's record EV demand is supportive for automakers with competitive electric lineups, while the global slowdown and especially North America's policy-driven decline keep deliveries and pricing risk elevated.
marketImpact.timeframe: Over the next 2-4 weeks as Q3 reports and October delivery data arrive

tickers.rationale: Europe's demand supports the EV category, but a regional split and fierce price competition mean aggregate market growth does not guarantee Tesla share gains.
The Volkswagen Group has a large European footprint and its electric share expanded in the region; follow-through depends on margins and new registrations.
Record European demand may help exporters, but China's weaker domestic market and rising exports can bring both volume opportunity and pricing pressure.
